note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — MAT + FLOWER SEX
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1253) — Follow the surface runners through the mat. In the Flora, under Buchloe dactyloides, the pollen-bearing heads rise above the leaves while the bur-like seed-bearing heads usually hide among them.

Buffalograss is a low warm-season perennial spreading into sod by aboveground stolons. Confirm the horizontal runner and rooting node on the SAME plant; the existing mat photo does not expose roots. Flowering plants are usually dioecious: male branches stand above leaves, while female bur-like clusters stay low. Rare mixed-sex plants occur. Species panels 1–2 show a Texas male plant and male heads; panel 3 is a comparison image, not a local female voucher.
tiles.short: Trace an actual creeping stolon, then distinguish raised male combs from concealed female burs.
tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROWTH/SEX CUES; ROOTED RUNNER + LOCAL FEMALE MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: At the inside blade–sheath junction separate the actual ligule from long side hairs. South Dakota State describes a hair fringe <1 mm, while a regional Colorado treatment describes a ~0.5–1 mm ciliate membrane; record this source wording rather than asserting an exact membrane edge from the photograph. Species panel 4 is a real Jim Conrad Texas collar view, but no millimeter ruler establishes ligule length. Photograph the free inner margin at 10–20×.
tiles.short: Short hair-fringed or ciliate-membranous ligule, generally less than ~1 mm.
tiles.status: REAL COLLAR PHOTO; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED INNER LIGULE

tiles.heading: 03 · MALE — COUNT SHORT COMBS AND SPIKELETS
tiles.details: On an attached flowering culm, count the comb-like unilateral branches rather than assuming every comb is a spikelet. Flora of North America describes 1–3(4) branches; South Dakota State gives 2–5 branches about 7–13 mm long. Kew reports male spikelets ~4–5.5 mm, with two florets and two glumes. Existing Texas panels 1–2 visibly show male heads and anthers, not calibrated glumes or floret dissections.
tiles.short: Raised male heads: often 1–3(4) short one-sided branches, each carrying 2-flowered spikelets.
tiles.status: REAL MALE COMBS PRESENT; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SCALED ATTACHED SPIKELET

tiles.heading: 04 · MALE — SEPARATE GLUMES AND LEMMAS
tiles.details: Dissect a mature MALE 2-flowered spikelet under a 1-mm scale. South Dakota State reports unequal male glumes about 1.4–3 mm and <5 mm; Kew reports ~4–5.5 mm whole male spikelets and 3-veined awnless male lemmas. Do not transfer FEMALE hardened-glume teeth to a male lemma, or draw vein arrows on intact comb photos. Record male anther color only where visible.
tiles.short: Male glumes unequal, roughly ~1.4–5 mm across sources; lemmas 3-veined, without long awns.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MALE ANATOMY; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — DISSECTED GLUMES/LEMMAS

tiles.heading: 05 · FEMALE — OPEN A HEALTHY BUR
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1253) — Part the leaves near the base and look inside the swollen sheath for the bur-like head. The Flora gives usually 3–5 spikelets, each with one floret.

Seek intact, healthy female heads hidden in foliage, not the conspicuous male combs. Kew describes female spikelets ~3–4 mm, a hardened ~3–4 mm upper glume with a three-part apex, and a 3-veined fertile lemma ~2.5–3.5 mm; the lower glume is much reduced or obscure. Flora of North America describes bur-like branches ~2.5–4.5 mm with often 3–5 spikelets. The comparison triptych's CENTER is fungus-altered and must NEVER be presented as normal female anatomy. Female glume teeth are not equivalent to a long awn on a male lemma.
tiles.short: Low female clusters contain one-flowered spikelets; hardened upper glumes form three-toothed burs.
tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED FEMALE ANATOMY; NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — HEALTHY TEXAS FEMALE + DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC GATE
tiles.details: Blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis) generally carries 1–3 prominent curved eyebrow-like branches rather than separate male comb and concealed female bur morphologies. Curlymesquite (Hilaria belangeri) also forms stoloniferous mats but has a different reproductive head. Introduced bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has radiating slender terminal racemes and a hair-fringed collar. Require a linked rooted runner, opened ligule and sex-verified reproductive organs; all six archived source-specific photo licenses and the seven-panel gallery still require public-rights and responsive arrow QA. Keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Blue grama's curved terminal eyebrows and bermudagrass's fingers differ from buffalograss's sex-specific heads.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: START AT GROUND LEVEL: Buffalograss is a short stoloniferous sod-forming grass. When flowering, look for raised pale comb-like MALE heads (two well photographed by Jim Conrad in Uvalde County), then search deeper among the short leaves for VERY DIFFERENT compact FEMALE bur-like clusters (shown in a licensed source comparison: LEFT normal female, RIGHT normal male, MIDDLE fungus-infected abnormal plant). Usually sexes occur on separate plants, but mixed-sex exceptions exist. Unlike blue grama's prominent curved eyebrows, the soil-level runners/sex-specific heads are stronger buffalograss clues. An attached rooting stolon with node remains unphotographed.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST at soil: find a LOW connected mat. Photograph ACTUAL creeping aboveground stolon with the true node and any attached adventitious roots; existing mat image does not demonstrate roots.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At the inside blade–sheath junction separate the actual ligule from long side hairs. South Dakota State describes a hair fringe <1 mm, while a regional Colorado treatment describes a ~0.5–1 mm ciliate membrane; record this source wording rather than asserting an exact membrane edge from the photograph. Species panel 4 is a real Jim Conrad Texas collar view, but no millimeter ruler establishes ligule length. Photograph the free inner margin at 10–20×.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Buffalograss is a low warm-season perennial spreading into sod by aboveground stolons. Confirm the horizontal runner and rooting node on the SAME plant; the existing mat photo does not expose roots. Flowering plants are usually dioecious: male branches stand above leaves, while female bur-like clusters stay low. Rare mixed-sex plants occur. Species panels 1–2 show a Texas male plant and male heads; panel 3 is a comparison image, not a local female voucher.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Blue grama has a prominent curved terminal rooster-comb inflorescence and generally forms a tuft or short rhizomatous crown, while buffalograss spreads by stolons and has distinct male and female heads. Curlymesquite also mats but often has visibly hairy stolon nodes and a different flower head. Bermudagrass often has several finger-like racemes and an introduced lawn-grass context; stolons alone are not proof of buffalograss.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: MALE = RAISED COMBS, pollen. FEMALE = LOW GREEN BURS. MIDDLE infected Commons photo = ABNORMAL, not the female key. BOTH SEXES CAN OCCASIONALLY SHARE A PLANT. STOLO(N) = creeping aboveground runner with rooting nodes (still needs a confirmed macro).

The sex-comparison triptych is EXTERNAL ONLY and includes a fungus-infected central panel; six physically stored JPEGs are verified in the canonical species folder. The normal female still needs a source-verified local macro.
